title: Advanced RPA (UiPath Orchestrator and Enterprise Automation)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Advanced RPA (UiPath Orchestrator and Enterprise Automation) ##### The bot that processed one invoice 4,000 times An insurance back office deployed a UiPath bot to key claim data into a mainframe terminal. It read a folder of PDFs in a loop, processed each, and moved on. On night eleven, the mainframe session dropped mid-transaction on invoice 847. The bot's `Try/Catch` wrapped the entire loop, so the exception unwound everything and the workflow restarted from the beginning — reprocessing 846 already-completed invoices. Then it hit 847 again, crashed again, and restarted again. By morning it had performed roughly 4,000 duplicate entries and the reconciliation took a week. The design error is architectural, not incidental: **a single loop with no transactional boundary, no queue, and no distinction between a broken record and a broken system.** Enterprise RPA solved these problems years ago with the dispatcher/performer pattern and Orchestrator queues. Knowing that pattern is what separates a demo bot from a production one. ##### Robust selectors and UI resilience Everything in RPA rests on identifying UI elements reliably, and this is where most maintenance cost lives. UiPath selectors are XML-ish descriptors of a control's position in the accessibility tree: ```xml ``` The rules that make selectors survive: - **Prefer stable attributes** — `automationid`, `name`, `aaname` — over `idx`. An index shifts the moment someone adds a field. - **Wildcard volatile parts.** `title='Claim Entry - *'` tolerates a changing claim number in the window title. - **Use anchors.** The **Anchor Base** activity locates an element relative to a stable neighbouring label, which survives repositioning. - **Strict versus fuzzy selectors** — modern UiPath offers both; fuzzy matching with a similarity threshold tolerates minor text changes at some risk of matching the wrong control. - **Never use image or coordinate matching** unless the accessibility tree genuinely offers nothing (Citrix, remote desktops). OCR and image matching break on resolution, theme and DPI changes. Pair selectors with **explicit waits** — `Element Exists`, `Wait For Ready`, `Retry Scope` — never fixed `Delay` activities. A hard-coded three-second wait is simultaneously too slow on a fast day and too short on a slow one. ##### Attended versus unattended, revisited for production Attended bots run on a person's machine, triggered by them, foreground, able to pause for input. Unattended bots run on dedicated VMs, triggered by schedule or queue, headless, and must handle every exception alone. The production implications of unattended operation are what matter here: credentials cannot be typed interactively (hence Orchestrator **Assets**), work must be recoverable if a VM dies (hence **queues**), and every failure needs classification because no human is present to judge (hence **exception types**). ##### Orchestrator: the control plane UiPath **Orchestrator** is what converts individual bots into a managed fleet. Four capabilities matter most. **Queues** hold work items as **transactions**. A robot requests the next item, processes it, and reports success or failure. Orchestrator tracks status (`New`, `In Progress`, `Successful`, `Failed`, `Retried`, `Abandoned`), enforces retry counts, deduplicates on a **Reference** field, and supports deadlines and priorities. This is the fix for the opening story. With a queue, invoice 847 fails as a *single transaction*; 1–846 remain `Successful`; the robot picks up 848 next. No restart, no duplicates. **Assets** store configuration and credentials centrally — encrypted, environment-scoped, and changeable without editing the workflow. A credential asset injects username and password into the bot at run time, so nothing sensitive lives in the process. **Schedules (triggers)** launch processes by time or by queue activity. Queue triggers are particularly useful: spin up robots when items appear, scale to a configured maximum, and idle otherwise. **Machines and robots** define the execution fleet, with licensing and concurrency controls. ##### REFramework: dispatcher and performer The **Robotic Enterprise Framework** is UiPath's production template, and its core idea is separating work *discovery* from work *execution*. **The dispatcher** finds work and pushes it into the queue. It does nothing else — no processing, no keying. It reads the invoice folder, extracts a reference and the data, and adds one queue item per invoice. **The performer** loops: get one transaction from the queue, process it, report the outcome, repeat until the queue is empty. ```text DISPATCHER (runs hourly) 1. Read folder / API / database for new work 2. For each item: Add Queue Item (Reference = invoice_number, deduplicate on it) 3. Log count added PERFORMER (queue-triggered, N robots in parallel) INIT open apps, read Assets, verify environment GET Get Transaction Item from queue → null? go to END PROCESS Try: key data into legacy app verify saved Set Transaction Status = Successful Catch BusinessRuleException as bre: Set Transaction Status = Failed, Type = Business (no retry — the data is wrong) Catch Exception as ex: Set Transaction Status = Failed, Type = Application (Orchestrator retries automatically) close and reopen the application (clean state) END close apps, send summary ``` Why this structure is worth adopting wholesale: - **Transactional granularity.** One failure affects one item. - **Horizontal scaling.** Five performers consume the same queue in parallel with no coordination code — Orchestrator hands each robot a distinct item. - **Automatic retries** on system exceptions, configured per queue rather than coded. - **Deduplication** via the Reference field, enforced by Orchestrator. - **Recovery.** A performer VM that dies leaves its item `In Progress`; Orchestrator reclaims it after a timeout. - **Clean state between transactions** — the init/close cycle prevents one bad transaction corrupting the next. ##### Business versus system exceptions This distinction is the assignment's focus and it is the most important classification in RPA. A **Business Rule Exception** means the *data* is wrong. The invoice is missing a PO number; the claim amount exceeds the policy limit; the customer ID does not exist. **Retrying will fail identically**, because nothing about the environment will change. Route it to a human queue for correction, with the reason attached. A **System Exception** means the *environment* failed. The application crashed, the terminal session dropped, an element was not found, the network timed out. **Retrying may well succeed**, because these conditions are transient. Let Orchestrator retry, and reset application state before the next attempt. ```vb ' Inside the PROCESS state of a performer Try ' --- Business validation FIRST, before touching the target app --- If String.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(in_TransactionItem.SpecificContent("PONumber").ToString) Then Throw New BusinessRuleException("Missing PO number on invoice " & invoiceRef) End If If CDec(in_TransactionItem.SpecificContent("Amount")) > policyLimit Then Throw New BusinessRuleException("Amount exceeds policy limit") End If ' --- System interaction --- Process_Invoice(in_TransactionItem) SetTransactionStatus(in_TransactionItem, QueueItemStatus.Successful) Catch bre As BusinessRuleException Log.Warn("Business exception: " & bre.Message) SetTransactionStatus(in_TransactionItem, QueueItemStatus.Failed, ErrorType:=QueueItemErrorType.Business, Reason:=bre.Message) AddToHumanReviewQueue(in_TransactionItem, bre.Message) ' no retry Catch ex As Exception Log.Error("System exception: " & ex.Message) SetTransactionStatus(in_TransactionItem, QueueItemStatus.Failed, ErrorType:=QueueItemErrorType.Application, Reason:=ex.Message) TakeScreenshot(invoiceRef) ' diagnostic evidence CloseAllApplications() ' reset to a clean state ' Orchestrator will retry per queue configuration End Try ``` Two practices embedded there. **Validate business rules before touching the application**, so bad data never causes half-finished UI interactions. And **screenshot on system exception** — a headless failure at 3 a.m. is nearly impossible to diagnose without one. ```mermaid flowchart TD D[Dispatcher: hourly] -->|Add Queue Items
dedup on Reference| Q[(Orchestrator Queue)] Q --> P1[Performer 1] Q --> P2[Performer 2] Q --> P3[Performer 3] P1 --> T{Process transaction} T -->|success| S[Status: Successful] T -->|BusinessRuleException| B[Status: Failed / Business
→ human review, NO retry] T -->|System Exception| E[Status: Failed / Application
screenshot + reset apps] E -->|retries < max| Q E -->|retries exhausted| A[Alert + dead-letter report] S & B & A --> R[End-of-run summary] ``` ##### Power Automate Desktop and Automation Anywhere **Power Automate Desktop** is bundled with Windows and integrates natively with the Microsoft ecosystem. Its equivalent of Orchestrator is the Power Platform admin centre with machine groups and cloud-flow triggers. Weaker on queue semantics and enterprise governance than UiPath, but often free-at-the-margin for Microsoft-heavy organizations and entirely adequate for departmental automation. **Automation Anywhere** is cloud-native with a similar control-room model, strong in finance and healthcare. The pattern transfers regardless of vendor: **discover work, queue it, process transactionally, classify failures, retry only the retriable.** Vendors differ in tooling, not in the correct architecture. ##### Hybrid RPA and API The most valuable judgment in enterprise automation is knowing that **RPA is a bridge, not a destination**. Surveys of the field (Syed et al., 2020) consistently characterize it as a tactical layer over systems that cannot be changed. So design hybrid from the start: - **API wherever it exists** — reading source data, writing to modern systems, sending notifications. Faster, testable, and it does not break when a button moves. - **RPA only for the specific screens that have no alternative** — usually one legacy application in an otherwise modern chain. - **Keep the RPA surface as small as possible.** A process that pulls data via API, transforms it in code, uses RPA for the single legacy keying step, then writes results via API has one-tenth the maintenance burden of an all-RPA equivalent. A concrete hybrid shape: an n8n workflow receives the trigger, calls APIs for enrichment, and pushes items into an Orchestrator queue via the UiPath API. Performers do only the legacy keying. Results flow back through the API. Each tool does what it is best at, and every year the RPA portion should shrink as vendors expose more APIs. ##### Common pitfalls - **Looping over work in one workflow** instead of using a queue — the 4,000-duplicate story. - **Index-based selectors** that break on any layout change. - **Fixed `Delay` activities** rather than conditional waits. - **Catching all exceptions identically**, retrying bad data forever. - **Credentials in the workflow** instead of Orchestrator Assets. - **No state reset** after a system exception, so the next transaction inherits a broken UI. - **No screenshots on failure**, making unattended debugging guesswork. - **Missing Reference field**, so re-running the dispatcher duplicates the queue. - **Automating a process nobody simplified first** — RPA amplifies bad processes. - **Using RPA where an API exists** because nobody checked. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a **UiPath dispatcher/performer over an Orchestrator queue** that processes invoices, **retries failed items**, and **routes business versus system exceptions differently**. Test both paths explicitly — feed in one invoice with a missing PO number (should fail as Business, no retry, land in review) and one that fails because you closed the target application mid-run (should fail as Application, retry, and succeed on the next attempt). The mini project is that pipeline made concrete: read invoices from a folder, key them into a legacy application, and **retry failed items via Orchestrator**. If you do not have a legacy application, Notepad or the Windows Calculator is a perfectly legitimate stand-in for learning selectors, waits and state reset — the architecture is what matters. For the assignment, **separate business from system exceptions and route each differently**, and explain the reasoning: business exceptions are deterministic data problems where retrying is guaranteed to fail and a human must intervene; system exceptions are environmental and transient where retrying with a reset state is likely to succeed. Show the queue in Orchestrator afterwards, with items in both failure categories and the retry history visible. ##### Key takeaways - Queues give transactional granularity: one bad item fails alone, the rest continue, and Orchestrator handles retries, deduplication and reclaim. - The dispatcher/performer split separates finding work from doing it, enabling parallel robots and clean per-transaction state. - Build selectors on stable attributes with wildcards and anchors, and use conditional waits — never indexes, coordinates or fixed delays. - Business exceptions mean bad data (route to humans, never retry); system exceptions mean a broken environment (retry after resetting application state, and screenshot for diagnosis). - Treat RPA as a deliberately shrinking bridge: use APIs for everything possible and confine UI automation to the screens that genuinely have no alternative.
